lesson.title: Supersonic and Broke: Why the Concorde Never Made Financial Sense
lesson.summary: The Concorde was a genuine engineering triumph that could fly passengers across the Atlantic in about three and a half hours, and it was also, almost from the start, an economic failure whose development costs were never recovered.
lesson.body:
The Concorde was a joint British and French program to build a supersonic passenger airliner, first flying in 1969 and entering commercial service in 1976. It worked. Cruising at roughly twice the speed of sound, it could cross the Atlantic in about three and a half hours, compared to roughly seven or eight hours on a conventional subsonic jet, and for most of its operating life it had a strong safety record. This is not a story about the physics or the engineering failing, unlike cold fusion the underlying science was completely real, and unlike Theranos nobody was lying about what the machine could do.

Where Concorde failed was economics, and the failure was not subtle. Development costs ran to a large multiple of the original government estimates, and in the end only about twenty aircraft were ever built, with roughly half entering commercial service, far short of the hundreds of orders originally hoped for. Most airlines that had placed early options on the plane cancelled them once the true operating economics became apparent. The two airlines that actually flew it, British Airways and Air France, effectively received their aircraft written down in value or subsidized by their governments, because no airline would have paid a price that reflected the actual cost of developing the plane.

The operating economics were brutal in their own right. Concorde burned far more fuel per passenger than a subsonic widebody jet, which hurt badly once the oil price shocks of the 1970s hit. Its sonic boom meant many countries, including the United States, banned supersonic flight overland, which effectively restricted its routes to ocean crossings. Its narrow cabin held around a hundred passengers, well below what a widebody jet could carry, which limited how much revenue any single flight could generate. To have any chance of covering costs, tickets had to be priced at or above first class fares, which confined the market to a small number of wealthy business travelers rather than the mass market that would eventually make international air travel affordable. Concorde was retired in 2003, not long after a fatal crash near Paris in 2000 and a post-2001 downturn in air travel made an already weak business case even weaker, having never come close to recovering its development costs.

This is a good place to connect back to the earlier chapter on opportunity cost. Every dollar, pound, and franc, along with the engineering talent, that went into making a supersonic jet fly could have gone toward the kind of aviation research that instead produced highly efficient, high-capacity subsonic widebody jets, the technology that actually did make intercontinental travel affordable for ordinary people, rather than a luxury reserved for a few thousand wealthy travelers a year. There is even a term for a closely related psychological trap that Concorde lent its name to: the Concorde fallacy, a version of the sunk cost fallacy where a project keeps getting funded specifically because so much has already been spent on it, rather than because of what it will actually deliver going forward, and government support for Concorde continued for years after its economic problems were well understood.

The lesson to carry forward is distinct from the previous two chapters. Concorde is not a story of scientific error like cold fusion, or of fraud like Theranos, the plane genuinely flew and did exactly what its engineers said it would do. It shows that a technology can be a complete technical success and still be an economic failure, a distinction worth holding onto for any expensive emerging technology, quantum computing included, where the engineering could eventually work while the business case around it still might not.
